articles.title: ‘The New Stanford Prison Experiment’ Creators Break Down Its Shocking Finale
articles.summary: “The New Stanford Prison Experiment” ends on a far more hopeful note than Stanford psychology professor Philip Zimbardo’s original 1971 trial. The first iteration of the Stanford prison experiment took 24 white male college students (save one Asian American) and paid them $15 a day to participate…
body: Over the course of the experiment, five people bow out — the first of whom, Larry Foy, a former convict who goes by the nickname “Scary Larry,” gets severely triggered by being in a prison environment again and demands to be removed. “Nobody thought it would affect him in the way that it did, but we knew he could make the decision for himself and relieve himself of the experiment if it became too much, which he in fact did,” Lipsitz explains to Variety. “I think he was surprised by how much it affected him.”

The experiment nearly unravels by day six (again) when two prisoners, Pete and Brandon, are placed in “23 and 1” for conspiring against the guards, meaning they must remain locked in their cell for 23 hours and a day and are given 1 hour a day outside it for showering and recreation. Brandon nearly bails, but decides to stay after an emotional phone call with his mother. “We thought it would end on the same day that the original experiment did,” admits Lipsitz, adding that the Pete and Brandon predicament raises an interesting question for audiences: “Do you see them as ridiculous pains in the ass or antiheroes?”

articles.title: ‘Clayface’ Director James Watkins Explains That [SPOILER] Cameo, Introducing Gotham City to the DC Universe and All the Shape-Shifting Kills
articles.summary: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for “Clayface,” now playing in theaters. Batman fans will have to wait patiently for the next installment in Matt Reeves and Robert Pattinson’s Caped Crusader saga, but they can get a peek at the rebooted DC Universe’s Gotham City in “Clayface.”…
body: Clayface has appeared in many Batman comics through the years, and he’s a classic villain who’s made the crossover into animated shows and video games. This version of him has also technically already appeared in the rebooted DC Universe in James Gunn’s animated series “Creature Commandos,” but now the monster gets his own origin story and live-action debut. The movie also gives the first look at Batman’s hometown of Gotham City in the new DC Universe. Gunn’s “Superman” kicked things off in Metropolis last year, but now another one of DC’s most famous cities gets unveiled in “Clayface.”
With Variety, Watkins explains finding the final Clayface monster look, recruiting Paul for his cameo and creating Gotham City.
The Clayface name has been used by several villains in Batman comics. How did you land on the Matt Hagen version instead of the first iteration, Basil Karlo?
This is the first time we’re seeing Gotham in the rebooted DC Universe. Did you have a specific year or time you wanted to set the world in?

articles.title: Sam Fender calls out ticket prices ahead of tour
articles.summary: The Geordie singer appears to have lowered ticket prices ahead of his upcoming tour.
body: Sam Fender has said he has removed a ticket category from sale after being unhappy with pricing for his upcoming tour.
The 32-year-old announced his Proper Massive Stadium Tour earlier this week, which will visit Newcastle, Cardiff, London, Edinburgh, Dublin and Manchester in summer 2027.
While tickets are yet to go on sale, Fender responded to a post on social media which claimed to outline the expected ticket prices.
The Geordie musician now appears to have lowered the prices and said the "costs are astronomical compared to two years ago" but he could not control the venue or ticketing fees.

articles.title: ‘A Court of Thorns and Roses’ Gets a Fittingly Sexy Fashion Collection Ahead of Sarah J. Maas’s Latest Book
articles.summary: In an age of endless brand partnerships and collaborations, it always feels good seeing a team-up that doesn’t feel forced. Such is the case with For Love & Lemons very sexy collaboration with “A Court of Thorns and Roses” — a collection of corsetry, lace, romantic florals and embellished evening…
body: The Spring Court-inspired pieces feature pastel florals and delicate lace, including the $639 Rose of the Manor Gown, while the darker Night Court assortment includes the $629 Night Court Mini Dress and $829 Moonveil Gown. Elsewhere, celestial-inspired Starfall designs and nods to characters like Nesta and the Valkyries round out the collection, with pieces ranging from a $398 beaded mini skirt to a $729 gown.

“This collection has been over a year in the making, and it was born out of true passion,” For Love & Lemons co-founder Gillian Kern said of the partnership. “We love the way Sarah J. Maas uses fashion to evoke a mood.”

The collection also includes several pieces featuring custom embroidery, hand-beaded detailing and intricate embellishments. Produced in limited quantities, the designs will not be restocked once sold out, according to the brand. Several styles, including the Storykeeper Dress and Dance with Fire Gown, have already sold out, while other pieces remain listed as coming soon.

articles.title: Former ’60 Minutes’ Executive Producer Bill Owens Joins Creator Media Company Newpress
articles.summary: Owens will be EP of the new firm, which raised money from Emerson Collective and media veterans Jesse Angelo, David Leavy, Brent Montgomery and Patrick Steel.
body: Former CBS 60 Minutes executive producer Bill Owens is getting into the creator economy.
The veteran journalist is joining the media startup Newpress as its EP.

Newpress was founded by Johnny and Iz Harris, who are both established YouTube filmmakers (the company includes Johnny Harris’ current YouTube channel). The company is planning to launch a handful of new shows over the next few months, with a longer-term goal of having 12-16 channels led by creators who are subject matter experts.
Owens will work with all of the creators to develop new shows and bolster their production. It is his first role since exiting 60 Minutes last year.

articles.title: Dark Matter Creator Blake Crouch 'Wasn't 100% Convinced' To Do Season 2 — Until They Wrote One Specific Episode [Exclusive]
articles.summary: Black Crouch, showrunner of Apple TV's Dark Matter, tells us that he wasn't convinced about a second season until he and his team wrote one specific episode.
body: How do you follow up a season of television that already adapted everything from the source material? Not easily, as it so happens. "Dark Matter" mastermind Blake Crouch finds himself in the unusual position of being the author behind the original 2016 book and, remarkably enough, the lead creative on the Apple TV adaptation of his own work. So when news first broke that another season had been greenlit to continue the story beyond the pages of the book, many fans (us included) wondered the same thing: What the heck could "Dark Matter" Season 2 be about?

If that was tough for us fans to wrap our minds around, it was nothing compared to the struggles Crouch and writing partner Jacquelyn Ben-Zekry experienced while figuring out where to take the multiverse-traveling journey of Jason Dessen (Joel Edgerton) and his family next. "We had originally pitched the show as a three-season show, although we didn't know — obviously, you don't know that it's going to be great," Crouch told me during a recent Zoom interview. "And we knew the first season was going to be the full book, then we would see what happened."

articles.title: Busan International Film Festival 2026 Wrap-up
articles.summary: A recap of this year's Busan International Film Festival.
body: Getting to the port city was a bit of a trek: I flew a little over 14 hours to Hong Kong and another 3 hours to Busan. I stayed in the Haeundae district, an area with bustling nightlife, colorful food stalls, packed bakeries, and exciting bars. That meant I needed to take the Busan Metro from Haeundae to Centum City, the festival’s home base.

The cinema center is a sprawling, silver, Frank Gehry-esque structure made up of three smaller, interconnected buildings (Cine Mountain, Biff Hill, and Double Cone) with screening rooms, masterclasses with the likes of Na Hong-jin and Lav Diaz, a dense library, concessions, activations, and more. A winding bridge binds them around a semi-open-air theater that boasts the world’s largest cantilever roof, whose underside is animated by LED lights featuring a flush of colors and even cartoon robots. Bustling pavilions surround the center, with food trucks selling Yakisoba, Takoyaki, Tteok-twi-sun, nachos, pizza, churros, and more.

articles.title: Mapping The Galaxy: The Four Galactic Quadrants In Star Trek Explained
articles.summary: You've probably heard Star Trek characters throw around terms like "Gamma Quadrant" or "Beta Quadrant." Here's what to know about how the galaxy is divided.
body: Welcome to Trekspertise, a series where we break down the technology, history, details, and decisions that make the Star Trek universe so complex — and so fun.

There are four quadrants in the "Star Trek" universe, named after the first four letters of the Greek alphabet: Alpha, Beta, Gamma, and Delta. When stellar cartographers on "Star Trek" decided to map the Milky Way, they sliced it into four pieces, just to keep things clear.

"Star Trek" stays bound almost entirely to the Milky Way galaxy. The distances between stars are so unbelievably vast, even the fictional starship engines concocted for the franchise aren't powerful enough to traverse those distances in any practical amount of time. Indeed, the vast bulk of the action on "Star Trek" takes place in the Alpha Quadrant, the portion of the galaxy where Earth happens to be situated. According to "The Star Trek Encyclopedia," Earth is also close to the Beta Quadrant border.
Humans, Vulcans, Andorians, and most members of the Federation all hail from the Alpha or Beta Quadrants. Ditto the Klingons and Romulans, who have empires situated mostly in the Beta Quadrant.

articles.title: Anthony LaPaglia: ‘There is not a role I didn’t get that I ever gave more than four hours of grievance to – even Tony Soprano’
articles.summary: The actor on surviving 2000s network television in Without a Trace, the role that made him take Brad Pitt seriously, and leaving the US to ‘ride out Trump’ Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email. I didn’t know before reading your new memoir that you were almost Tony Soprano.
body: It’s not Tony Soprano. There is not a role that I didn’t get that I ever gave more than four hours of grievance to. When I don’t get something, I move on. Because there’s no point. I’m very pragmatic that way. It’s for your own mental health. Once it’s gone, it’s gone.
If you were casting your dream project with three actors you’ve already worked with, plus one new face, who would be on your team?
Allison Janney. Kerry Armstrong. Alison Whyte. And a new face … I just saw Moneyball and I don’t think I ever took Brad Pitt that seriously but that guy is phenomenal. Great movie.
Acting opposite Janney in A View from the Bridge on Broadway sounds as though it was a transcendental experience for you.

articles.title: 5 Best Movies Like Clayface
articles.summary: From classic body horror tales to twisted supervillain origin stories, here are the five best movies to watch if you enjoyed DC's Clayface.
body: The DC Universe has expanded with not just a new film, "Clayface" directed by James Watkins, but a whole new genre: horror. Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries), a former poor kid from Gotham City who has grown up into a rising star in the film industry, makes a big mistake when he sleeps with a gangster's girlfriend. His face mutilated, Hagen's rise pivots into a devastating fall. Desperate to get his life back, he opts for an experimental treatment by Dr. Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie) that slowly makes his face as changeable as clay.

"Clayface" pulls from the proud tradition of body horror films where a normal person experiences a physical and often horrific transformation, losing their humanity in both mind and soul. At the same time, even if it plays out more like a horror film than a superhero film, it's still based on a DC Comic. So here are five films that are perfect follow-up watches to "Clayface," with the aim of recommendations as concoctive a blend as the movie's own genre influences.
If there's one movie bound to scratch the same itch as "Clayface" — and scratch it even better — it's Sam Raimi's 1990 "Darkman," which /Film's review of "Clayface" compared said film to.
